references.text: The parable of the unjust judge and the persistent widow shares the same theme: perseverance and persistence in prayer lead to an answer, even if the motive is not goodwill but persistence.
A direct continuation of the teaching on prayer: 'Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.' This supports the point that persistent prayer is answered.
The immediate context: the parable of the friend who comes at midnight asking for bread. Verse 8 is the main point and conclusion of this parable.

Jesus' parallel teaching in the Sermon on the Mount about asking, seeking, and knocking, with the assurance that God gives good gifts to those who ask Him – the same principle regarding God's willingness to answer persistent prayer.

The unjust judge grants the widow justice 'because she bothers me so' – exactly the same principle as in Luke 11:8, where the friend gives because of persistence (ἀναίδεια), not because of friendship.
Abraham prays persistently for Sodom and negotiates with God down from fifty to ten righteous people. An Old Testament example of persistent, enduring prayer that is heard.
Jacob wrestles with God and refuses to let go until he receives a blessing – an OT example of persistence and perseverance being rewarded.

Proverbs warn against laziness using the image of sleep and rest – in contrast to the parable where the man must get up from bed, highlighting the value of not letting slothfulness hinder one from helping.
The call to approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and find grace for help at the right time connects to Jesus' teaching on boldness and persistence in prayer.
Paul urges believers to persevere faithfully in prayer and to watch in it with thanksgiving – a practical application of the principle of perseverance in prayer from Jesus' parable.
